newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 29.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- NORTHERN ELECTRIC FACES NEW HOSTILE BID

Northern Electric on Monday became the target for its second hostile bid since the failed effort in 1994/1995 by Trafalgar House. Independent US power company CalEnergy initiated a takeover bid worth some 766 million stg. In a highly successful dawn raid, the company also secured 13 percent of the shares in Northern. Analysts say that Northern may have something of a fight on its hands this time round.
-- BT TO OFFER INTERNET ACCESS WITH TOUCH-SCREEN TERMINALS

British Telecom is planning to invest 50 million stg in developing a series of touchscreen terminals that will offer customers access to the Internet. Users accessing the Touchpoint terminals will be able to avail of a range of services, including flight booking and electronic retailing. As many as 10,000 such access points are planned and BT has signed up a range of companies keen to exploit electronic commerce.
-- FORSHEDA INVESTOR GROUP TO REJECT TI BID

It has emerged that investors controlling almost 30 percent of the shares in Swedish polymer group Forsheda are opposed to a takeover bid worth 189 million stg from Britain's TI Group. Henderson Investors and four other institutional investors in the company are set to reject TI's cash offer as inadequate. These investors are expected to seek talks with Forsheda and TI's advisers, SBC Warburg.
-- SWISS BANKS ALLOW PROBE OF 'NAZI GOLD' ACCOUNTS

A consortium representing Swiss banks has announced that it will allow an in-depth inquiry into their role in the handling of stolen gold and other valuables deposited by the Nazis during the Second World War. A series of accountancy firms seeking the contract to carry out an audit have been provided with a memorandum setting out the terms of reference for the inquiry. An initial audit involving four banks is due to be completed by mid-1997, with the full investigation finished by 1998.
-- 'NO NEW FULL-TIME JOBS FOR 10 YEARS'

A report from independent consultancy Business Strategies predicts that of the 1.5 million new jobs expected to be created over the next decade in Britain almost none will be full-time. Half will be part-time positions, with the rest being accounted for by self-employment. The consultancy has said that this situation is unlikely to change even if Labour win the next general election. About 80 percent of the part-time positions to be created are expected to be filled by women.
-- RUSH TO QUALIFY FOR EMU CONDEMNED

The head of the Dutch central bank, Wim Duisenberg, and also the man who will be responsible for the transition to a single European currency, has warned that the speed with which countries are rushing to qualify for participation risks undermining the euro. Duisenberg has expressed particular concern about the extraordinary measures being adopted by some EU member states to satisfy certain Maastricht criteria, while also warning other factors were not receiving enough attention.
-- EU MINISTERS PRESS COMMISSION FOR MORE BEEF AID

Farm ministers from across the EU on Monday called on the European Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler to increase the amount of aid being provided to farmers affected by the continuing BSE crisis. The call comes amid signs that aid provided to date has been eroded by the continuing pressure on beef prices and demand. Britain, meanwhile, is calling on the commission to allow the export of beef from herds which have been certified as being free from BSE.
-- PENSIONS 'SHOULD BECOME EMU CRITERION'

The all-party Commons social security committee has called for the level of unfunded pension liabilities in each EU member states to be taken into account when judging whether or not they qualify for participation in the single European currency. In a report due out later in the week the MPs on the committee will call for Britain and other EU member states to annually publish the level of pensions not covered by specific assets.
-- CABLE INDUSTRY REJECTS BSKYB CHARGE PLANS

The British cable industry has rejected a new set of charges on offer from BSkyB for the supply of programming. The offer came in response to pressure from the Office of Fair Trading, which had previously examined complaints from companies in the sector regarding allegedly unfair pricing practices. The Cable Communications Association, meanwhile, has hired the services of a legal firm to challenge the new proposals and is reported to be determined to fight the issue all the way to the European Court if necessary.
